trading-basics.question: What makes the price of something in a market go up?
options: More people want to buy it than want to sell it at the current price
The broker decides to raise it
Prices only go up at the start of the month
A trading signal group posts about it
trading-basics.explanation: Prices move because of supply and demand. When buyers are more eager than sellers, price rises until they balance again.

trading-basics.question: Which statement about trading is most realistic for a beginner?
options: You can double your money every month if you follow signals
Losing trades are normal, and protecting your capital comes first
With enough indicators you will never lose
Trading is easy once you open a live account
trading-basics.explanation: Every trader has losing trades. Beginners who focus on learning and managing risk last much longer than those chasing quick profits.

trading-basics.question: What is the main difference between trading and gambling?
options: There is no difference
Trading always makes money
Trading uses a plan, defined risk and review, while gambling relies on luck without an edge or plan
Gambling is done online and trading is not
trading-basics.explanation: Trading without a plan or risk limits can look a lot like gambling. A written plan, a stop-loss and honest review are what make it a skill to study.

trading-basics.question: What does it mean to 'go long' (buy)?
options: You expect the price to go up
You expect the price to go down
You hold the trade for at least a year
You use the largest possible position
trading-basics.explanation: Going long means buying because you expect price to rise. Going short means selling because you expect price to fall.

trading-basics.question: Where should a complete beginner practise first?
options: A live account with borrowed money
A demo (practice) account with virtual money
A friend's account
Nowhere; just start trading live
trading-basics.explanation: A demo account lets you learn the platform and practise your plan without risking real money.

reading-price-charts.question: On a candlestick, what does the body show?
options: The range between the open and close price
The broker's spread
The number of traders
The highest price of the week
reading-price-charts.explanation: The body spans the open and close. The thin lines (wicks) show the high and low.

reading-price-charts.question: Why is a single candle not enough to make a decision?
options: Candles are random
Context such as trend, support and resistance gives the candle meaning
Only line charts are accurate
Candles only work on the daily chart
reading-price-charts.explanation: The same candle shape can mean different things in different places on the chart. Always read it in context.

risk-management.question: Your account is $500 and you risk 1% per trade. What is your maximum risk on one trade?
risk-management.explanation: 1% of $500 is $5. The position-size calculator turns that into a lot size for your stop-loss distance.

risk-management.question: A trade risks 20 pips to target 40 pips. What is the risk/reward ratio?
risk-management.explanation: You risk 1 unit to make 2 units, so the ratio is 1:2. At 1:2 you break even if you win about 33% of trades (before costs).

risk-management.question: Where should a stop-loss go?
options: Wherever feels comfortable
At a level on the chart where your trade idea is proven wrong
Never use a stop-loss
Exactly 1 pip from your entry
risk-management.explanation: Place the stop where the idea is invalid. Then size the position so that hitting the stop costs only your planned risk.
